articles.title: APOD: 29 October 2026 – The Horns of Venus
articles.excerpt: APOD Science APOD APOD: 29 October 2026 – The… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. The Horns […]
articles.content: Explanation: That’s no moon. But you could be forgiven for thinking it was a crescent Moon in the sky. It is a lesser known fact that Venus also has phases. (What about other planets?) The featured image shows Venus seen almost directly between the Sun and the Earth. This happens once every year and a half, and it is like the alignment that happens every month during a new Moon. But the new Moon is dark, while Venus’ backlit atmosphere refracts and scatters the sunlight, creating a glowing crescent arc that extends beyond 180 degrees: the tips of this arc are called the “horns”. The crescent can be seen with a small telescope or binoculars during twilight, but those with exceptionally acute eyesight may be able to see it with the unaided eye. Ancient Babylonian astronomers may have been the first to study Venus’ brightness changes, which are related to its phases. Many other cultures have similar astronomical records, including the oldest surviving Maya book.

articles.title: Arnab Strikes India
articles.excerpt: The first named storm of the North Indian Ocean’s cyclone season made landfall along the coast of Andhra Pradesh.
articles.content:
The first named storm of the 2026 North Indian Ocean cyclone season—Arnab (pronounced Or-nab)—emerged in the Bay of Bengal on October 25, a rather late start for a basin that typically produces named cyclones in April or May.

When the VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) on NOAA-20 captured this nighttime image at 20:12 Universal Time on October 26 (1:42 a.m. India Standard Time on October 27), the storm had sustained winds of about 140 kilometers (85 miles) per hour, according to the India Meteorological Department (IMD).

When Arnab made landfall on the Andhra Pradesh and Yanam coast early on October 28, sustained winds were 130 kilometers per hour. IMD categorizes a storm that strength as a “very severe cyclonic storm,” which is similar to a Category 1 storm on the Saffir-Simpson hurricane wind scale. It made landfall between Bapatla and Visakhapatnam, a heavily settled area home to large cities, farmland, and fishing communities.

Arnab caused extensive damage, uprooting trees, inundating crops and homes, limiting fishing operations, and disrupting transportation and power networks, according to news reports. Prior to landfall, Indian authorities had evacuated tens of thousands of people from vulnerable coastal areas. 

The storm comes in the midst of an El Niño, a climate pattern marked by warmer-than-normal water temperatures in parts of the equatorial Pacific that emerges roughly every two to seven years. The changed ocean conditions can influence the atmosphere in ways that alter global weather patterns and change the distribution of rainfall, winds, tropical cyclones, fires, floods, and other phenomena.

In the Bay of Bengal, for instance, some research indicates that altered environmental conditions during an El Niño are associated with a reduction in tropical cyclone activity. The ocean basin sees both less frequent and less intense tropical cyclones during El Niño years, researchers have found.

articles.title: Caltech Names Artemis II Commander Reid Wiseman as NASA JPL Deputy
articles.excerpt: Artemis II Commander Reid Wiseman has been named Caltech associate vice president and deputy director of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. The emeritus astronaut and retired U.S. Navy captain begins his new role at NASA’s center of excellence for robotics and deep space exploration and at Caltech, which manages JPL for NASA, on […]
articles.content:
Artemis II Commander Reid Wiseman has been named Caltech associate vice president and deputy director of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. The emeritus astronaut and retired U.S. Navy captain begins his new role at NASA’s center of excellence for robotics and deep space exploration and at Caltech, which manages JPL for NASA, on Nov. 30, 2026.

“Reid has spent his career at the edge of what is possible, and he has the technical judgment, operational experience, and leadership to help push that edge farther,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “As commander of Artemis II, he helped carry America back around the Moon, and now, as an emeritus astronaut, he will continue giving back to NASA from a new vantage point at JPL. Reid is joining a storied laboratory that has made an enormous amount of history, and there is a lot more ahead. I am excited to see what he and the JPL team accomplish in the years to come.”

During the Artemis II test flight, Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch, and Jeremy Hansen journeyed 695,081 miles on a lunar flyby that took them farther than any humans have ever traveled before.

“It feels fitting for Reid, who with the Artemis II crew traveled farther from Earth than any human in history, to join Caltech and JPL — institutions that for nearly 90 years have sent spacecraft into the far reaches of our solar system and beyond,” said Dave Gallagher, JPL director and Caltech vice president. “Reid shares our drive for discovery, knows what it takes to lead teams through high-stakes missions, and has a remarkable ability to inspire people everywhere. He adds incredible bench strength to our leadership team as we build on the lab’s legacy and shape its future together.”

After joining NASA’s astronaut corps in 2009, Wiseman went on to serve as flight engineer aboard the International Space Station for the 165-day Expedition 41 mission in 2014 and was a commander of NASA’s 21st Extreme Environment Mission Operations expedition, during which he lived for eight days in a habitat on the ocean floor in 2016. As the agency’s chief astronaut from December 2020 to November 2022, Wiseman led NASA’s astronaut corps, overseeing crew flight readiness and crew safety for all NASA human spaceflight missions. During his years of service at the agency, he has conducted hundreds of scientific experiments.

“I’ve explored the furthest reaches of what a human can explore at NASA — and there were truly no words in the English vocabulary to describe seeing the Sun disappear behind the Moon from deep space. But that experience was really the jumping off point to go do the impossible things that Caltech and JPL dream, dare together, and do for NASA and the nation,” Wiseman said. “What an awesome time in my career to join this team and to try and push humanity and push our understanding of the solar system and the universe.”

Wiseman joins JPL, NASA’s only federally funded research and development center, as the lab approaches its 90th anniversary since being founded by Caltech. In his role as Caltech’s associate vice president and JPL deputy director, Wiseman will be responsible for the strategic leadership, stewardship and continuous improvement of laboratory operations, including close partnership with Caltech on institutional planning, management and compliance. Serving as Center Management Authority for JPL mission execution, Wiseman will ensure operational excellence across mission support functions in accordance with NASA requirements and applicable federal and state regulations. In addition, he will be JPL’s primary interface for national security programs.

“Reid brings to Caltech and JPL a truly unprecedented view of what humanity can achieve when ingenuity and determination are matched with the courage to pursue the furthest frontiers,” said Caltech president Ray Jayawardhana. “His pioneering spirit coupled with unbounded curiosity make him a natural fit for Caltech and JPL, a force-multiplier for a community whose daring continues to push the limits of humanity’s reach. I look forward to working closely with Dave and Reid as we chart our next era of exploration in partnership with NASA, elevating America’s space ambitions to breathtaking new heights.”

After receiving a bachelor’s degree in computer and systems engineering from Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, Wiseman joined the Navy, going on to fly combat missions and serve as a test pilot. He also has a master’s degree in systems engineering from Johns Hopkins University in his hometown of Baltimore.

articles.title: NASA Welcomes Vietnam as Newest Artemis Accords Signatory
articles.excerpt: The Socialist Republic of Vietnam became the 78th nation to sign the Artemis Accords, joining a growing coalition of like-minded nations committed to the peaceful, transparent, and responsible exploration of space.   “Vietnam is joining at an important point in the development of its own space program,” said NASA Deputy Administrator Matt Anderson in recorded remarks […]
articles.content:
The Socialist Republic of Vietnam became the 78th nation to sign the Artemis Accords, joining a growing coalition of like-minded nations committed to the peaceful, transparent, and responsible exploration of space.  

“Vietnam is joining at an important point in the development of its own space program,” said NASA Deputy Administrator Matt Anderson in recorded remarks for the ceremony. “NASA and the Vietnam National Space Center have built momentum in satellite innovation, land-use research, and radar-based Earth observation. Joining the Artemis Accords opens a new chapter in that relationship. We’ve aligned on the principles. The opportunities are in front of us, and now we can build on that foundation together. We are proud to welcome Vietnam to the Artemis Accords community.” 

Vietnam’s Minister of Science and Technology Vũ Hải Quân signed the Artemis Accords on behalf of the country during the Vietnam International Digital Week in Ha Long. The United States Ambassador to Vietnam Jennifer Wicks also participated in the signing event. 

Vietnam’s decision extends the U.S.-Vietnam Comprehensive Strategic Partnership into a new frontier.  Built on more than 30 years of cooperation, the partnership spans defense, economic, law enforcement, war legacy, and technological cooperation, and it advances peace, stability, and prosperity in a free and open Indo-Pacific. 

Earlier this year, NASA partnered with Vietnam’s Vietnamese-German University to support the agency’s Soil Moisture Active Passive mission, which measures surface-soil water worldwide. Vietnam also inaugurated its National Space Center in Hanoi and is developing domestic satellite capabilities through the LOTUSat program, focusing on Earth observation, weather monitoring, and disaster response. 

In 2020, NASA and the State Department joined with seven other founding nations to establish the Artemis Accords, responding to the growing interest in lunar activities by both governments and private companies. They introduced the first set of practical principles aimed at enhancing the safety and coordination between nations as they explore the Moon, Mars, and beyond. 

Signing the Artemis Accords means committing to explore peaceably and transparently, to render aid to those in need, to enable access to scientific data that all of humanity can learn from, to ensure activities do not interfere with those of others, and to preserve historically significant sites and artifacts by developing best practices for space exploration for the benefit of all.  

More countries are expected to sign the Artemis Accords in the months and years ahead, as NASA continues its work to establish a safe, peaceful, and prosperous future in space.  

Learn more about the Artemis Accords at:  

https://www.nasa.gov/artemis-accords

articles.title: Episode 185: NASA’s Flight Dynamics Facility
articles.excerpt: The Flight Dynamics Facility provides tracking data on spacecraft including the Orion crew capsule and the Roman Space Telescope. The facility’s history stretches back to the earliest days of Mercury, Gemini and Apollo. The post Episode 185: NASA’s Flight Dynamics Facility appeared first on NASA Science .
articles.content:
Host Andres Almeida: Every NASA mission depends on knowing where a spacecraft is at all times. 

At Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, the Flight Dynamics Facility provides that expertise, tracking everything from robotic science missions to crew capsules carrying astronauts. The facility’s history stretches back to the earliest days of Mercury, Gemini and Apollo. 

Today, its teams support missions including Artemis, the James Webb Space Telescope and now the Roman Space Telescope. 

In this episode of Small Steps, Giant Leaps, we talk with Sam Schreiber, former operations director for the Flight Dynamics Facility at Goddard. He takes us inside the work of tracking spacecraft, preparing for the unexpected, and applying lessons learned from one mission to the next. 

This is Small Steps, Giant Leaps. 

[Intro music] 

Welcome to Small Steps, Giant Leaps, the podcast from NASA’s Academy of Program/Project & Engineering Leadership, or APPEL. I’m your host Andres Almeida. 

Sam Schreiber is with us today. Hi Sam, thanks for making time today. 

Sam Schreiber: My pleasure. 

Host: Talk to me a bit more about the Flight Dynamics Facility. 

Schreiber: So, my formal title is the Flight Dynamics Facility Operations Director. So, I am one of two civil servants, a director and a deputy, that oversee the work that is done in the Flight Dynamics Facility. 

Host: Has the facility always been at Goddard? 

Yes, it is a Goddard resource. It has essentially existed in one form or another since the beginning of the space program. So, early days. We’re talking Mercury, Gemini, Apollo. 

There were two groups at Goddard. One group focused on flight dynamics and navigation of early science missions. The other group focused on early human spaceflight and making sure that all the antennas on the ground around the world were pointing at and able to acquire the Mercury, Gemini, and Apollo spacecraft as it flew around the Moon. 

Those two groups were combined in the early 1980s to form what is now known as the Flight Dynamics Facility. 

Host: That’s a long legacy, and now you have Artemis… 

Schreiber: That’s correct, yes. So, we have supported human spaceflight for years. Obviously, space shuttle, International Space Station, Commercial Crew, the cargo vehicles. As we’ve gotten into Artemis, it’s been a large effort for any tracking assets that the Near Space Network uses. So, this could be the TDRS satellites that are in geosynchronous orbit, looking down at the Earth. It could be antennas on the ground all around the world. 

Those antennas need a single source of trajectory truth to know where to point, when to point, in order to essentially talk to the astronauts, get their health and safety of the spacecraft for mission control in Houston to send commands to the spacecraft. So that’s, that’s our primary job. 

So, when the SLS lifts off the launch pad, any antennas that are pointing at the rocket ascending into space are doing so because we’re telling it where it’s going, and most importantly, not just where it’s going, where it might go in case there’s an abort, where it might go in case there’s some kind of off-nominal trajectory, and we can still talk to the astronauts if they end up landing in the North Atlantic or, or doing an abort once around the Earth.

Host: How soon in the life of a mission does the FDF get involved with trajectory design and analysis?

Schreiber: It depends on the mission. So, we support a wide range of missions. We support science missions. So, we’re about to launch the Roman Space Telescope, what, in two weeks? I know this is being recorded in August. And so, our teams are the flight dynamics experts that’ll get Roman Space Telescope off the ground and on its way to its Lagrange point orbit, and then we’ll fly for the rest of the missions. 

Science missions, it can depend. It can be as late as a year or two prior to launch. For something like the James Webb Space Telescope, which we also fly, it could be years beforehand because we had to get involved in the trajectory design of the mission, where and how it’s going to get out to its orbit. 

For human spaceflight, it’s very rapidly changing. You know, the Artemis III mission changed just a few months prior. It was going to launch a few years from now, now it’s launching next year. So, we’re involved immediately, and we are responding to all the changes that are happening right now. 

Host: With all these assets that require tracking, is there such thing as a typical day for you?

Schreiber: Yeah, I describe my role as closest to that of a CEO of a company, I’m involved in the day-to-day operations and making sure that the facility is up and running. You know, we had some actual power hits today. We hear, you know, alarms going off and batteries in the basement are kicking on. So just making sure that the facility is ready to support NASA, no matter what.

Part of it’s staffing and making sure we have the right staff and right staffing combination in the right skillsets. We need flight dynamics engineers to obviously do the flight dynamics, astrodynamics, orbital mechanics. We need software engineers and developers, software testers, IT people, IT security. So, it is, systems engineering, right? 

We need all these different skill sets all in one to run this ship, and on top of all of that, I have to make sure there’s the right amount of funding to do all that work, based upon all the different requirements from all the missions that come to us. 

So, my job is a mixed bag of drumming up business, you know, going to mission A, B, or C, saying, “You should use our facilities and our, and our expertise.” Or going to Headquarters and drumming up funding. It can also be managing the contract of the great people that do the work within the FDF, and changing some contract bits here or there to make sure the work is appropriately allocated. 

It can vary based, day to day, based upon what’s the emergency of the day, who’s reaching out for support. We need some analysis done for an orbital reentry that might happen. We need some analysis done of tracking data that might that might be needed for Artemis III, IV, or V. It really does vary, so kind of act as that interface for the technical teams. 

Host: Your job is many jobs. 

Schreiber: We all have many hats, don’t we? 

Host: Can you recall any moments when something didn’t go the way you expected but you learned from it?

Schreiber: In, I think it was 2015. So, I’ve been in the FDF for 13 years, seven years as a civil servant. So, prior to my time as deputy director, now director, I was in the contractor pool and doing the work in the FDF, and one of the missions I supported was DSCOVR [Deep Space Climate Observatory]. DSCOVR launched in, I think it was 2015, if I remember correctly. 

The plan for DSCOVR was to launch on a Falcon 9 out to a Lagrange Point, and the expectation from the flight project was that we would be able to acquire DSCOVR while still on the launch vehicle, while still thrusting up into space. 

So, what happens is the launch vehicle launches, the fairing deploys, so you have less mass. You’re out of the atmosphere, so you deploy the fairing, and then the spacecraft is exposed to space, so you can technically communicate with it. 

So, on one side of the coin, there’s an expectation that you’d be able to communicate with DSCOVR from the mission operations center as soon as the fairing came off. On the other side of the coin, there was no requirement for that, and there was an expectation that you would acquire the spacecraft after separation from the launch vehicle. 

So, if you imagine the vehicle is launching into space, it’s thrusting out toward [a] Lagrange point, and then eventually it stops thrusting and it kicks off, and the launch vehicle separates from DSCOVR. 

 So, acquisition didn’t actually happen as early as the mission operations center expected. We really needed to make sure we’re reviewing all requirements, that no requirements are mismatching or in conflict. If they are, we bring them up to the flight project or whoever the project is that we’re supporting. So that was a lesson learned that is now being folded in, by the way, to Roman, because there is an expectation that they will acquire the Roman Space Telescope while still on the launch vehicle, and we make sure that’s going to be, it’s going to happen. 

Host: What’s keeping the team busy right now? 

Schreiber: There’s a lot of work related to ensuring there’s the right-size budget for the next coming fiscal year, right? NASA’s budget is set by Congress, and we have to make sure we have the right budgets for the right work. 

And so, there’s a lot of negotiations in looking at each of our roughly 30 to 40 missions that we fly. I have this whole portfolio. Are the missions paying the right amount of money for their support? Are there changes in requirements that might drive some ups and downs? If there’s late-breaking requirements, that might be at risk because even if they throw us some money halfway through the year, I can’t go and hire, you know, two or three staff members to support that immediately. 

So, a lot of the work that happens on a day-to-day basis is negotiation and making sure we are right-sized for the work required of us. 

Host: How did you end up in this role? 

Schreiber: My first job out of grad school was at Johnson Space Center, working for a company called United Space Alliance. They no longer exist, but my job was guidance, control, and propulsion flight instructor for the space shuttle to NASA astronauts and flight controllers. 

I finish grad school, I do an internship out at Johnson, and then I end up working there for a number of years. You get trained how to train the astronauts, right? There’s a whole training program. There’s a specific division called the spaceflight training division, and that’s what I was a part of. 

So, I trained a number of astronaut crews on the space shuttle operations. It was a really, really neat job to show up every day, especially in your early-to-mid-twenties. Met a lot of interesting people. I trained some flight controllers in their, in their simulations as well. But the shuttle program came to an end, and in 2011 I found myself unemployed. 

So, at the time I was recently married, and my wife finished medical school, so she was looking for a residency, and she matched at Georgetown University Hospital. 

So, I moved to DC, and I was unemployed. I ended up being unemployed for a number of months, but finding my way to working for a private company called GMV. And GMV stands for Grupo Mecanico De Vuelos. 

It is a Spanish-based company out of Madrid, and they do flight dynamics, amongst other things. They do flight dynamics for the European Space Agency, and they had started a new arm of the company in the USA in Rockville [Maryland], near where I lived. So, I ended up randomly finding a job with them and learning flight dynamics, ground systems, and flight dynamics and navigation from them. 

Now, I knew nothing about this really about this stuff beforehand. My master’s degree is essentially a propulsion degree, so I learned Fortran and I learned Perl and I learned C++ (again), and what it means to navigate a spacecraft and to figure out where a spacecraft is and where it’s going. It was really interesting. [I] traveled around the world.

Their customers were commercial, as well as some government. So I worked on the GOES-R series spacecraft for NOAA. We were validating our ground systems with the specialists who know how to do the stuff from the FDF. That’s how I learned what the FDF even existed. 

And after a few years at the company, I applied for a job. 

Host: And did you take the Spanish language with you? 

Schreiber: No, no, no, not at all. 

[Laughter] 

It was really hard. So, it was really hard. I I learned Spanish in high school, right? And it would be really hard to call my colleagues in Madrid, which, of course, there’s a six-hour time difference, and trying to do technical Spanish. And I just, and my, my office mate was from Barcelona, so he has that accent on his Spanish, right? And I definitely, I got better. Like, I definitely got better, but then I didn’t really use it for years. 

Host: You have a lot on your plate already. So, Sam, what was your giant leap? 

Schreiber: What was my giant leap? One of the cool things that happened toward the end of the space shuttle program for me was, unfortunately, a bunch of the pilot-type astronauts were leaving. They saw that there was no more shuttle flights for them. The Constellation Program had been canceled, and Artemis was way in the future, and they were just leaving. 

But they needed to do what they called integrated simulations with mission control. This is where astronauts come, just kind of random astronauts picked from the astronaut office, come to the simulator, get in the shuttle simulator, and fly it. And instructors like myself would break things: kill an engine, cause a leak, whatever, during launch, during re-entry, during orbit, mostly launch and re-entry. And they still needed to do simulation runs. So, it all connected to mission control as if it was real. 

So, mission control would sit there in the flight control room as if it’s real data coming through, and we would do maybe 2,3,4,5 different simulation runs. 

And anyway, astronauts were leaving, and they there weren’t enough people in the pool to do those generic simulations. So, someone came up with the idea of what if we get a bunch of instructors, quote unquote, astronaut-certified for these simulations, so at least we can keep pushing forward? 

So, a number of us, I think it was eight or 10 of us, went through a series of training events with flight directors involved to make sure that we were kind of up to snuff to act as astronauts instead, and I was one of those people. I was trained in the pilot position, which is the righthand seat next to the commander. 

And so, there were a number of generic simulations where there’s an astronaut commander in my left, a mission specialist flight engineer behind me, and I’m in the pilot seat, and I’m sitting on my back in the space shuttle simulator, you know, throwing switches as if engines are failing and APUs are blowing up. That was really, really fun.

And I have applied to be an astronaut several times. I thought I can really do this job. I have obviously not been selected, but that felt like between that and sitting inside space shuttle Discovery before it launched for one of its missions, that was also, like, a peak moment. 

So, I felt like I kind of hit a peak, a giant leap peak, early, 20 years ago. But it was really, really neat, and it’s, it’s sustained me for many, many years.  

Host: And did the teams make you feel like a crewmember? 

Schreiber: They were exceedingly, exceedingly kind and graceful, and you know I even screwed up a little bit here or there, but did not make me feel bad whatsoever, and I, it was a dream come true at that point.  

Host: That’s an ideal team dynamic, where you make mistakes and still, they lift you up. 

Schreiber: Of course! 

Host: With so many teams and projects, how do you ensure lessons learned are lessons learned? 

Schreiber: Yeah, so, within the FDF itself, we do have a specific task order, a group of people that do operations planning and systems engineering, right? And the job is to be that connective tissue. We have requirements coming in, requirements going out. We have lessons learned. We have a lessons learned database. 

So, every time we do a mission, let’s say we’re about to launch Roman, and we get it out to its orbit and it gets into what’s called the Phase E, right? Just kind of keep, keep going on with your mission for the next several years. We’ll do a post-mission report and capture any lessons learned to the entire lifecycle of the mission up till now, and those go into a database. And so, that when we do the next thing, we are required to review that database as an entrance criteria for the next review. 

That’s part of the process, right, is to review whether it’s a root cause analysis or a lessons, just a lessons learned. You’re required to review those things as an entrance to the next operations readiness review that you might have for the next mission. 

Those also get fed up to the projects that we support. So, one of the big projects we support is the Near Space Network, and they provide services. Not only do they fly TDRS and make sure that there’s ground tracking, they also provide a lot of services to human spaceflight and launch vehicles. 

So, every time there’s a new launch vehicle or a new human spaceflight mission, you review lessons learned going into the network operations readiness review as part of the process. 

So, part of the, the lifecycle process is ensure you’re capturing lessons learned, putting them somewhere where you can and will review them as part of the next mission that will come up.

Host: That’s great. Sam, that’s our time. Thanks for coming onto the podcast and talking with us. 

Schreiber: I appreciate the opportunity to talk with you here today, share a little bit about what the Flight Dynamics Facility does and how we support the entire agency, whether it’s a science mission, a human spaceflight mission, a launch vehicle. We do a lot of various and different things. 

Host: That’s it for this episode of Small Steps, Giant Leaps. For a transcript and for all other episodes, visit nasa.gov/podcasts. While you’re there, check out our other podcasts like Houston, We Have a Podcast, Curious Universe, and Universo curioso de la NASA. As always, thanks for listening. 

Outro: This is an official NASA podcast.

articles.content:
One year ago, NASA’s Quesst mission made history with the first flight of the X-59 quiet supersonic research aircraft. Since then, the X-59 has completed 40 additional flights, marking a year of steady progress for the program.  

While its first flight on Oct. 28, 2025, focused on low, slow flights to conduct systems checks, the X-59 has since reached a maximum altitude of more than 56,000 feet and speeds up to Mach 1.53. 

The X-59 has spent the past year expanding its flight envelope, flying at the altitudes, speeds, and conditions that will be utilized for all aspects of the Quesst mission. The aircraft’s team will continue that work in the coming months, but also transition toward a new phase of testing: acoustic validation, which will focus on analyzing the sounds the X-59 makes.  

The X-59 is shaped so that when it flies at its intended quiet supersonic altitude of 55,000 feet and speed of Mach 1.4, people on the ground won’t hear a loud sonic boom – they’ll hear a thump projected to sound like a car door closing from about 20 feet away. During future flight tests, NASA will study and record those sonic thumps. 

NASA’s Quesst mission aims to help enable a new era of commercial supersonic flight over land, exploring the potential for a new market of faster air travel. Learn more about the Quesst mission on NASA’s site.

articles.content:
NASA’s Artemis III SLS (Space Launch System) core stage is integrated alongside the twin solid rocket boosters on Oct. 28 inside the Vehicle Assembly Building’s High Bay 3 at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida.  

Technicians lifted the 212-foot rocket stage from the facility’s High Bay 2 using a one-of-a kind lifting beam designed to place the stage onto the mobile launcher. Once testing and checkouts are complete, teams will roll the core stage and booster stack out to Launch Pad 39B to conduct a tanking test where liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen fuel will be loaded only into the core stage and launch teams will practice countdown procedures and timelines.  

The Artemis III mission will launch NASA astronauts Randy Bresnik, Frank Rubio, Andre Douglas, and ESA (European Space Agency) astronaut Luca Parmitano in the Orion spacecraft on top of the SLS rocket to test rendezvous and docking capabilities between Orion and commercial spacecraft from Blue Origin and SpaceX ahead of future mission to land astronauts on the Moon.

articles.title: NASA University Challenge Ignites Trajectory of Drone Entrepreneur
articles.excerpt: Five years ago, Gavin Gardner was a Michigan State University engineering student researching next-generation drone technology as part of a NASA grant. Garder expected the research to be demanding – but he was surprised that navigating the financial side of the work presented an even greater challenge. Although Gardner was used to leading fellow students […]
articles.content:
Five years ago, Gavin Gardner was a Michigan State University engineering student researching next-generation drone technology as part of a NASA grant. Garder expected the research to be demanding – but he was surprised that navigating the financial side of the work presented an even greater challenge.

Although Gardner was used to leading fellow students in a lab setting, he and his team were completely new to things like creating budgets, handling large sums of money, and promoting their work for crowdfunding.

That’s why demonstrating both engineering and entrepreneurship skills are major tentpoles of NASA’s University Student Research Challenge (USRC), an initiative that provides grants to teams of college students interested in helping the agency realize its aeronautical research goals.

“Half the battle is building your product,” Gardner said recently. “The other half is selling the product in a way that everyone else can understand what you’re doing and not talking in nerdy, engineering ways.”

Gardner and his Michigan State USRC alumni teammates are still using those lessons today, as aerospace developers. In 2024, they founded their own company, AG3 Labs, which specializes in drones for military training exercises.

“I don’t think I would discredit our technical expertise in getting us to where we are today, but I know that USRC was a booster that really amplified our trajectory at such a young age,” Gardner said.

NASA USRC manager Steven Holz said Gardner’s experience shows what students can accomplish when they receive both a grant and guidance – enabling a future workforce and contributing to the aviation industry.

“We are proud to see the success of USRC alumni,” Holz said. “We hope that every team that participates in the program sees, like Gavin, how they can grow technically, entrepreneurially, and use the opportunity as a launchpad for their own innovative careers.” 

Research path

Gardner’s path to running his own company began with a middle school age trip to Space Camp, where he began realizing that he wanted to be an engineer.

The engineering bug also bit his brother, Gryson Gardner, and the two of them would often be found in their Michigan garage tinkering with various machinery, including drones and electronic kits.

When Gardner arrived at Michigan State, he looked for extracurricular groups and found one dedicated to the increasingly popular hobby of drones. He gained hands-on, practical experience in how drones are made and operated.

In 2021, Gardner received an email from a friend who told him they had just won a USRC grant from NASA for an activity called Aerial Intra-city Delivery Electric Drones (AIDED), and they needed help building a new drone.

“We had this idea that instead of flying through the whole city, why can’t a drone just hitchhike a ride on a city bus like everyone else does?” Gardner said.

The concept was for a cargo-carrying drone to take off, dock on top of public transportation such as a bus, charge its batteries while riding along, and then take off for its final leg of the delivery. The team built and flew a full-scale drone to prove the concept but decided against pursuing a commercial venture.

“The commercial drone market kind of scared us a little bit with the large number of regulations that go into operating such a novel idea like this with flying over people in a dense city,” Gardner said.

But the team’s demonstration of technical prowess and confidence led to a second USRC award from NASA in 2023 – the Laser Energized Aerial Drone System (LEADS), which focused on using a laser to transfer power directly to a drone in flight.

While working on LEADS, which led to flying a prototype, Gardner’s network of contacts within the drone community expanded to include NASA personnel at the Glenn Research Center in Cleveland, who made him aware of internship opportunities, which he applied for and was accepted while in graduate school.

Student challenge paves way for opportunity 

As his graduation in the spring of 2025 with a master’s degree approached, Gardner took the initial steps in late 2024 to co-found with his brother and other USRC alumni AG3 Labs after a friend suggested the military could use low-cost drones to test effective counter drone systems.

An initial award from the U.S. Army led to more contracts, allowing the company to expand and ramp up its operations, where today their production capability enables thousands of drones to be built each month.

Gardner credits his experience with USRC, especially when it came to learning more about the business side of running a technical operation, with helping create the opportunities for success he and his team are experiencing today.

articles.title: Astronauts Are Go For Thursday’s Power Upgrade Spacewalk
articles.excerpt: Mission managers have given the go for Thursday’s spacewalk to install a new roll-out solar array on the International Space Station’s port-side truss structure. The post Astronauts Are Go For Thursday’s Power Upgrade Spacewalk appeared first on NASA Science .
articles.content:
Mission managers have given the go for Thursday’s spacewalk to install a new roll-out solar array on the International Space Station’s port-side truss structure. Expedition 75 flight engineers Anil Menon of NASA and Joshua Kutryk of CSA (Canadian Space Agency) will set their spacesuits to battery power at 8 a.m. EDT signifying the start of their spacewalk for about six hours and 45 minutes of external maintenance. NASA+ begins its live spacewalk coverage at 6:30 a.m.

On Thursday, the spacewalking duo will first unbolt the roll-out solar array from a temporary stowage platform. Next, Menon will carry the roll-out solar array to the truss worksite while riding the Canadarm2 robotic arm. Kutryk will the translate to the port truss worksite while tethered to the orbital outpost and join Menon to complete the installation job. Finally, mission controllers will remotely activate the roll-out solar array to begin generating power.

Menon and Kutryk began their shift on Wednesday finalizing their spacewalk procedure reviews. Afterward, the pair inspected their spacesuits’ life support systems, communications gear, and other components ensuring their readiness for Thursday’s excursion.

After lunchtime, Menon and Kutryk joined NASA flight engineers Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney for a final spacewalk conference with specialists on the ground. Watkins and Delaney also familiarized themselves with lighting conditions and camera locations on the outside of the space station in order to monitor the spacewalkers and operate the Canadarm2. Finally, all four astronauts gathered at the end of their shift for a conference with robotics engineers to discuss Canadarm2 operations planned for the spacewalk.

Roscosmos’ three cosmonauts had a light duty day on Wednesday keeping up their science activities and familiarizing themselves with Thursday’s spacewalk operations. Station commander Pyotr Dubrov uninstalled multi-wavelength Earth photography gear that autonomously captured Pacific and Atlantic Ocean landmarks during the crew’s sleep shift. Flight engineer Sergey Teteryatnikov installed a different set of Earth imagery gear for another overnight session to photograph Pacific islands and South American glaciers, meanwhile, flight engineer Anna Kikina jogged on the Zvezda service module’s treadmill to test her fitness in microgravity.

Learn more about station activities by following the space station blog, @space_station on X, as well as the ISS Facebook and ISS Instagram accounts.

articles.title: NASA Selects 19 New Citizen Science Proposals in 2026
articles.excerpt: So far, 2026 has seen a flood of successes for volunteers who do NASA science, exemplifying NASA’s commitment to gold-standard science—transparent, reproducible and intrinsically collaborative. The Zooniverse platform, […]
articles.content:
So far, 2026 has seen a flood of successes for volunteers who do NASA science, exemplifying NASA’s commitment to gold-standard science—transparent, reproducible and intrinsically collaborative. The Backyard Worlds: Planet 9 project announced that their project volunteers have now discovered most of the known brown dwarfs, celestial objects that are similar to planets. The Zooniverse platform, with grant from NASA, reached a milestone of 1 billion classifications. Several projects have come online that leverage new super intelligence (SI) techniques to amplify or extend the work of volunteers. More NASA volunteers are using SI to build their own data tools and help write scientific papers than ever before.

Even with all of those achievements, our science community is already working on the next round of new volunteer projects and innovations. NASA’s Science Mission Directorate has selected nineteen proposals from research teams in 2026 that will result in new opportunities for you to do NASA science.

The Citizen Science Seed Funding Program

The Citizen Science Seed Funding Program (CSSFP-25) of NASA’s Science Mission Directorate aims to support scientists and other experts to develop citizen science projects and expand the pool of professional scientists who use citizen science techniques in their science investigations. Twelve new proposals to this program were selected.

“The Rogue Worlds Project: Activating volunteers to uncover the hidden population of super Jupiters with SPHEREx” led by Principal Investigator Jacqueline Faherty from the American Museum of Natural History. This project will invite you to search data from NASA’s SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer) mission to find free-floating planets and brown dwarfs in clusters of young stars. The SPHEREx space observatory mapping the entire sky in near-infrared wavelengths.

“Quantifying the calibrations between intrinsic galaxy merger timescales with visual pair/tidal-feature classifications” led by Principal Investigator Kameswara Bharadwaj Mantha of the University of Missouri. This project will investigate galaxy mergers, helping astronomers understand how galaxies evolve through time. You will be invited to classify realistic mock images of galaxies to help probe the statistics and dynamical evolution of galaxy mergers.

“Overlap Zoo; cosmic light tables for galaxy transparency” led by Principal Investigator Benne Holwerda of the University of Louisville. Galaxies, which glow with the light of the billions of stars they contain, also contain dust. This dust is easiest to see and quantify when it overlaps, or is backlit by, another galaxy. Help spot and characterize these rare overlapping galaxy pairs to help reveal how much dust they contain. Overlap Zoo is live! Follow this link to learn more and join the project.

“Planet Hunters Roman: Extending Citizen Science to Planetary Microlensing” led by Principal Investigator Bernard Gaudi of the Ohio State University. Exoplanets are planets orbiting stars other than our Sun. Their gravity can bend the light that travels around them. This project will invite you to spot exoplanets in data from NASA’s new Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope data by the way they bend starlight.

“Space Weather UnderGround: Deploying a low-cost Magnetometer Array with Citizens for Heliophysics Research” led by Principal Investigator Hyunju Connor at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center. Along with sunshine, our Sun produces the solar wind, an unrelenting flow of charged particles. Earth’s protective magnetic field shield deflects most of these particles, but not all, and not during extreme events. Help scientists monitor the subtle disturbances of Earth’s magnetosphere by the solar wind by setting up and monitoring your own magnetometer in Alaska.

“A Citizen Science Initiative for Sonified Plasma Wave Characterization” led by Principal Investigator Lauren Blum of the University Of Colorado, Boulder. “Plasma” is the name given to the ionized gases at the edge of Earth’s magnetosphere. Solar wind, the rain of charged particles that flows out from the Sun, can interact with and generate waves in the plasma. This project will turn data from this dynamic zone into sound signals. You will be invited to listen in to identify waves in the Earth’s magnetosphere.

“Revealing the Consequences of Foreshock Transients for Earth’s Magnetospheric System Through Participatory Science” led by Principal Investigator Wenli Mo at the Johns Hopkins University. This project will invite you to examine data from NASA’s MMS (Magnetospheric Multiscale) mission to identify “foreshock transients,”  phenomena that have a critical but poorly understood role in space weather. The resulting dataset will help reveal how foreshock transients form, their properties, and their impacts.  

“IMPACT: Interactive Magnetospheric Particle Analysis and Citizen Technology” led by Principal Investigator Muhammad Fraz Bashir at the University of California, Los Angeles. Energetic particles rain down from the magnetosphere into the upper ionosphere, heating and perturbing the ionosphere, disrupting the scatter of radio waves and GPS operations. This project will invite you to help match patterns between two types of data: measurements from satellites flying overhead that detect energetic particles raining down from space and measurements from ground-based instruments that detect electromagnetic waves. By comparing these patterns, volunteers will help scientists figure out which types of space waves are causing different kinds of particle precipitation, and in turn, help scientists better understand and predict disruptions to GPS and increased radiation risks during space weather events.

“Unlocking Clues About Particle Acceleration and Transport Using Particle Distributions” led by Principal Investigator Gang Kai Poh at the Catholic University Of America. NASA’s Advanced Composition Explorer, Parker Solar Probe, and Solar Orbiter are complementary missions gathering data to help scientists improve understanding of the Sun, solar wind, and space weather. Examine data from these missions to contribute to the study of the complicated flow of energetic particles from the Sun.

“Data Fusion in Space: Combining Citizen Observations to Classify Solar Wind Tracers” led by Principal Investigator Cynthia Lopez-Portela of the University of Maryland, Baltimore County. This project will invite you to use their pattern-recognition skills to spot features in images of the Sun’s corona, where the solar wind begins. These features can be used as tracers to help scientists track the movement of the solar wind and build better models of how it behaves.

“Mapping Lunar Iron Abundance Hotspots to Enable In-Situ Resource Utilization of Regolith Consolidation Technologies” led by Principal Investigator Karen Martirosyan at the University of Texas, Rio Grande Valley. Building a base on the Moon will require creative use of Moon materials. So what materials will future teams of astronaut base-builders have to work with? This project will invite you to help locate iron deposits in data from NASA’s Moon Mineralogy Mapper mission to help understand how the Moon formed and to aid future exploration.

“Small Body Discovery and Outburst Monitoring with a Worldwide Citizen Science Telescope Network” led by Principal Investigator Ariel Graykowski at the SETI Institute. This project proposes to activate a global network of citizen scientists, each equipped with a standardized small-aperture telescope, to conduct follow-up observation of cometary outbursts and small moving bodies (comets, near-Earth asteroids, and main-belt asteroids). With their global distribution and a program of twilight observations, amateurs will complement professional surveys. The project will develop systems to automate processing of contributed images and to distribute alerts for objects of interest to the network.

The Science Activation Program

The Science Activation Program (SciAct) from NASA’s Science Mission Directorate supports a portfolio of competitively selected, collaborative project teams that extend the impact of NASA science. These “SciAct Teams” accomplish this by connecting people and communities – many of whom would not otherwise meaningfully engage – with NASA science data and experts, local partnerships, and authentic science experiences. Seven teams selected in the latest round of competition will engage learners with citizen science efforts directly related to NASA research priorities. Several other selected teams plan to incorporate citizen science projects or community science projects (research efforts led by and focused on specific communities) into their work. 

The selected proposals include: 

“Growing Beyond Earth: Science Activation Through Distributed Space Crop Research” led by Principal Investigator Carl Lewis at Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden, Inc. To travel or live in space, humans will need to eat. Growing Beyond Earth trains and equips middle- and high-school classrooms to conduct growth experiments with seeds and crops being evaluated for use as space food.

“Sungrazer 2.0: From Armchair Discovery to Data-Driven Comet Science” led by Principal Investigator MaryKay Severino of the ARISA Lab and science lead Karl Battams of the Naval Research Laboratory. The original Sungrazer Project launched in 2006 in response to requests from citizen scientists for verification of comet discoveries. Since then, project volunteers have identified 5,204 comets and counting – the majority of known comets. Sungrazer 2.0 will bring the thrill of comet discovery to new audiences who will join the hunt for comets in images from NASA’s SOHO (Solar and Heliospheric Observatory) and STEREO (Solar Terrestrial Relations Observatory) missions.

“Discovering the SPARC: Space Physics through Amateur Radio Communications” led by Principal Investigator Nathaniel Frissell of the University of Scranton. Since 2017 amateur radio operators have worked together in the Ham Radio Science Citizen Investigation (HamSCI) community to study Earth’s ionosphere through carefully designed and conducted investigations of how their signals bounce off this high, ionized layer of Earth’s atmosphere. This project will bring hands-on space weather science to communities nationwide through amateur radio equipment and enroll high schools in a national research network.  

“Telescopes for All: Promoting audience engagement with NASA science via participatory data experiences using robotic telescopes” led by Principal Investigator Mary Dussault of the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory. This project will expand public access to a suite of 22 user-friendly, professional robotic telescopes. This access will allow people to observe, analyze, and contribute to NASA-aligned research, including the search and study of exoplanets and other citizen science projects. 

“Researchers Inspiring Public Participation in Lake Education and Science (RIPPLES)” led by Principal Investigator Sarah Yelton and science lead Tamlin Pavelsky, both at the University Of North Carolina, Chapel Hill. This project will collaborate with the Lake Observations by Citizen Scientists and Satellites (LOCSS) project to expand participation in lake and reservoir level monitoring. Submitted data will be used to validate observations such as those made by NASA’s SWOT (Surface Water and Ocean Topography) mission. 

“ARK (Antarctic Resilience and Knowledge): A Collaborative Network for Discovery and Education of Antarctica’s Iconic Species and their Changing Habitats” led by Principal Investigator Sharon Stammerjohn at the University of Colorado, Boulder. This project will invite you to examine NASA’s very high-resolution satellite images of Antarctica to study and monitor habitat changes affecting penguin, seal, and whale populations. With validation by scientists and integration of machine-assisted detection tools, this project will expand the analytical capacity of Antarctic researchers and build public literacy in polar ecosystem science. 

“Arctic Learning and Engagement with NASA Data for Community Solutions (Arctic LENS)” led by Principal Investigator Katie Spellman of the University of Alaska Fairbanks. This project will invite Alaskans to contribute seasonal environmental monitoring (snow, ice, aurora, spring ice-out, and green-up) in support of NASA missions including FORTE (Arctic Coastlines: Frontlines of Rapidly Transforming Ecosystems), SWOT (Surface Water and Ocean Topography), PACE (Phytoplankton, Aerosol, Cloud, ocean Ecosystem), and Landsat.

articles.title: Curiosity Blog, Sols 5043-5049: Preparing to Drill at ‘Nazca’
articles.excerpt: Written by Lucy Lim, Planetary Scientist at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center Earth planning date: Friday, Oct. 16, 2026 Following the Basque Lakes drill campaign, Curiosity has returned to a spot just a few meters away from the “Chiu Chiu” block to conduct our next drill campaign. “Chiu Chiu” itself wasn’t a good candidate for […]
articles.content:
Written by Lucy Lim, Planetary Scientist at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center

Earth planning date: Friday, Oct. 16, 2026

Following the Basque Lakes drill campaign, Curiosity has returned to a spot just a few meters away from the “Chiu Chiu” block to conduct our next drill campaign. “Chiu Chiu” itself wasn’t a good candidate for drilling but the block just beyond it was much more promising, so it became our drive target during Monday’s planning. I was on planning Friday as Geology and Mineralogy Science Theme Lead when we received our close-up views of the neighbor block from the post-drive imaging and our team was happy to see that it was jam-packed with the “disc- and needle-” shaped lumps, just like “Chiu Chiu.” We quickly gave the science go-ahead to proceed with preparations for drilling at the newly named “Nazca” site.

One major hypothesis about how the “discs and needles” texture formed is that the characteristic shapes were originally created during the growth of crystals, or “crystal forms.” Minerals will tend to grow into specific shapes depending on their microscopic crystal structure, similar to the salt crystals that you can grow in your kitchen as a home science project. (Maybe you have grown one of those for a science class in school!) The relatively large sizes of the crystal forms at “Nazca” and “Chiu Chiu” are providing clues about the temperature at the time when they grew and the availability of salts and fluids. However, we can’t necessarily assume that the modern-day composition represents the original mineral because sometimes mineral crystals are replaced by other minerals some time after original crystallization. The new minerals are then known as “pseudomorphs” because they have the same shape as the first minerals but not the same composition or molecular structure. 

As we prepared for the drill preload test, we also planned several special observations aimed at highly detailed characterization of the crystal forms. MAHLI will execute a Quantitative Relief Model (“QRM”) observation consisting of five overlapping images at slightly different geometries. The combination of these will enable a detailed three-dimensional relief model to be constructed. In addition, MAHLI will also add extra frames to its highest-resolution imaging by doubling the number of focus mechanism steps. Together, these observations will increase the resolution of the 3D models we will have of the crystal forms.

Meanwhile, the ChemCam LIBS will conduct a “depth profile” experiment to obtain compositional information from slightly deeper layers within a nearby crystal-form-rich target, “Toucan”. Normally the 150 LIBS laser shots from each sol’s observation are spaced out over a five-point raster at 30 shots per point, but this time we are concentrating all 150 laser shots on the same spot on the rock. Since each laser shot vaporizes a very small amount of the rock to form a plasma, the 150-shot profile should penetrate approximately five times deeper than a normal 30-shot point observation. We will thus be able to observe the composition deeper inside the exposed crystal form and see whether it’s different from the surface-level composition. There are several reasons this could be the case including exposure of the surface to the modern Martian environment and also the circumstances in which the crystal form developed originally, so it’s an experiment worth pursuing.

The LIBS, DRT and APXS will also be applied to the “Nazca” spot before the preload test to characterize its surface composition as thoroughly as possible before drilling. The third LIBS of the plan will go to “Condor,” a nearby block in which a finely layered texture is exposed.

We also continued to observe the modern Martian environment as twilight cloud season begins. In this plan we included some nighttime imaging of the larger and brighter of Mars’ two satellites, Phobos. Capturing images of Phobos and the nearby sky when Phobos is full can show sunlight reflecting off the moon and scattering in the Martian atmosphere, providing a good way to estimate the particle sizes in the Martian clouds. We can do similar measurements sometimes with solar observations, but the Phobos data allow us to measure cloud particle sizes later in the night. We expect to be measuring high-altitude carbon dioxide (CO2) clouds in this observation.

articles.content:
Explanation: Jupiter is one of the least lonely planets in the Solar System, at least when it comes to natural satellites. 115 moons have been discovered orbiting Jupiter so far! (Saturn has the most with 293, but who’s counting.) Ganymede and Io, two of Jupiter’s Galilean moons, met in the sky on October 20th, 2026. Today’s video captures the meeting, with Ganymede briefly blocking Io from view. This event, when an astronomical object passes in front of another and either completely or partially blocks it, is called a mutual occultation. The mutual occultations of Galilean moons are rare to witness because they require Earth’s edge-on view of their orbits. This occurs once every 6 years when Jupiter reaches its equinox and appears less “tilted”. Ganymede is also casting its shadow on Jupiter’s right side. Any fictional Jovian species within the shadow would experience a solar eclipse!
